findings.claim: the availability heuristic (recent or vivid events loom larger than base rates)
findings.failure_mode: gloss beyond the deep ref: 'vivid' and 'base rates' appear in neither the deep ref nor the source; 'recent' is in the source but not the deep ref
findings.evidence: Deep 148 carries only the Table 7.3 definition ('decision is based upon either an available precedent or an example that may be faulty'). Source 12953-12955: 'a decision based on an example, information, or recent experience that is that readily available to you, even though it may not be the best example'. 'base rate' absent from source.
findings.fix: correct: the availability heuristic (a readily available example or recent experience stands in for a better one) | cycle-to-deep: Ch 7.3 prose definition, source 12953-12955 ('an example, information, or recent experience that is ... readily available to you, even though it may not be the best example to inform your decision')

findings.claim: Interviewing as soon as possible and prohibiting counterfactual framing ("but we should have known...") are the direct procedural responses.
findings.failure_mode: premise imported from another source: the deep ref gives no link between hindsight bias and interview timing or counterfactuals; both moves are LFUO's (Handout C 'interview as soon as possible'; Part 9 'Avoid Counterfactual Arguments'), uncited here
findings.evidence: Deep 146 (definition only). LFUO deep 213 (hindsight bias -> interview as soon as possible, keep them on their own perspective) and 184 (avoid counterfactuals). Psych 2e source 15357-15359 (Ch 8.3): 'The reconstructive nature of memory contributes to hindsight bias (Carli, 1999)' supports a time-link but is not in the deep ref.
findings.fix: correct: LFUO's procedural responses (interview as soon as possible; avoid counterfactual arguments; LFUO Handout C, Part 9) are the direct counters; Psychology 2e supplies the mechanism | cycle-to-deep: Ch 8.3 'Memory Errors' bullet, source 15357-15359 ('The reconstructive nature of memory contributes to hindsight bias (Carli, 1999)')

findings.claim: participants weight vivid or recent incidents more than base rates
findings.failure_mode: same gloss as D001: 'base rates' and 'vivid' not in source or deep ref; 'recent' source-only
findings.fix: correct: participants reach for the readily available example or recent experience even when it is not the best guide to this incident | cycle-to-deep: as D001

findings.claim: Schacter's seven sins include suggestibility and bias: "current beliefs reshape memories" (Ch 8.3, Table 8.1).
findings.failure_mode: deep-ref paraphrase set in quotation marks and cited to a table, so it reads as the source's words
findings.evidence: Deep 183 gives '*bias* (current beliefs reshape memories)' as its own gloss, unmarked. Source Table 8.1 (15230): 'Memories distorted by current belief system' / 'Align memories to current beliefs'.
findings.fix: correct: Schacter's seven sins include suggestibility and bias, in which current beliefs reshape memories (Ch 8.3, Table 8.1)

findings.claim: Open-ended narrative questions ("walk me through what you were seeing") produce more accurate accounts.
findings.failure_mode: an inference from the misinformation effect stated as an empirical finding; neither the deep ref nor the source compares open-ended questions for accuracy ('open-ended' does not occur in the source)
findings.evidence: Deep 186: leading questions can alter eyewitness memory (Loftus and Palmer) [BT]. No accuracy claim for open-ended questions.
findings.fix: correct: Open-ended narrative questions ("walk me through what you were seeing") avoid planting the theory that the misinformation effect shows leading questions can plant.

findings.claim: Perception involves "both bottom-up (data-driven) and top-down (knowledge- and expectation-driven) processing"
findings.failure_mode: deep-ref paraphrase (with its parenthetical glosses) set in quotation marks as if source wording
findings.evidence: Deep 99 is paraphrase, unmarked. Source 8706-8709: 'Perception involves both bottom-up and top-down processing. Bottom-up processing refers to sensory information from a stimulus in the environment driving a process, and top-down processing refers to knowledge and expectancy driving a process'.
findings.fix: correct: Perception involves both bottom-up (data-driven) and top-down (knowledge- and expectation-driven) processing (Ch 5.1, "Perception") — drop the quotation marks

findings.claim: decisions made during the alarm or exhaustion stages are not comparable to decisions made at optimal arousal
findings.failure_mode: conflates two frameworks: GAS stages describe the body's response to a stressor over days to months (the exhaustion stage is depletion leading to illness), not in-incident decision quality; the arousal-performance link is Yerkes-Dodson's
findings.evidence: Deep 373: GAS alarm (immediate) / resistance (sustained) / exhaustion (depleted resources, illness or death). Source 27770-27786: resistance illustrated at 72 hours, exhaustion at 'three months'; 27788-27790: GAS is 'a response-based conceptualization of stress, focusing exclusively on the body's physical' responses. Deep 228: Yerkes-Dodson.
findings.fix: correct: decisions made under very high arousal (the alarm reaction, or distress rather than eustress; Ch 14.1) are not comparable to decisions made at the arousal level the Yerkes-Dodson law predicts is optimal for a complex task (Ch 10.1)

findings.claim: Open-ended questions over yes/no (TC 25-20 Ch 4) is the practical application of the misinformation effect (Ch 8.3); discovery-frame over critique-frame is the application of fundamental attribution error (Ch 12.1)
findings.failure_mode: relationship overstated: TC 25-20 gives its own rationale (defensiveness, participation) and explicitly recommends 'open-ended and leading questions', which sits in tension with the misinformation effect; its critique contrast is single-viewpoint vs multi-viewpoint, not an attribution argument
findings.evidence: TC deep 134 ('Open-ended questions are also much less likely to put him on the defensive. This is more effective in finding out what happened'), 126 ('Use open-ended and leading questions'), 15/35 (critique 'only gives one viewpoint'). Psych deep 186, 275-276.
findings.fix: correct: TC 25-20 prescribes open-ended over yes/no questions because they invite narrative and reduce defensiveness (Ch 4, "Summary of Recent Events"); Psychology 2e's misinformation effect (Ch 8.3) adds a memory reason and cautions against the TC's 'leading questions' where they embed a causal theory. The TC's AAR-not-critique stance (Ch 1; Ch 4) pairs with the fundamental attribution error (Ch 12.1): a single-viewpoint critique invites dispositional verdicts.

findings.claim: Scrum's Transparency pillar requires honest accounts; Psychology 2e ... provides the mechanism-level argument for why psychological safety is a precondition, not a nice-to-have
findings.failure_mode: attributes to Psychology 2e an argument about psychological safety that neither its deep ref nor its source contains ('psychological safety' occurs in neither); Scrum's Transparency is about visible process and artifacts, loosened to 'honest accounts'
findings.evidence: No 'psychological safety' in psych deep or in source (grep count 0). Scrum deep 37: 'The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work'.
findings.fix: correct: Scrum's Transparency pillar requires the emergent process and work to be visible (Scrum Theory, "Transparency"); Psychology 2e explains the cognitive and social forces (conformity, obedience, the fundamental attribution error) that work against that visibility even in teams committed to it

findings.claim: Roese and Vohs's research on hindsight bias is presented via the Psychology 2e text, not held directly in this corpus.
findings.failure_mode: fabricated borrowed-through citation: 'Roese' and 'Vohs' do not occur anywhere in the 47,143-line converted source or in the deep ref; the source attributes hindsight-bias research to Carli (1999)
findings.evidence: grep -c -i Roese = 0, Vohs = 0 in sources/converted/openstax-psychology-2e.md. Source 15359: 'The reconstructive nature of memory contributes to hindsight bias (Carli, 1999)'.
findings.fix: correct: Carli's (1999) work linking reconstructive memory to hindsight bias is presented via the Psychology 2e text (Ch 8.3) | cycle-to-deep: source 15357-15359 Carli (1999) bullet

findings.fix: correct: Clinical content (Ch 15–16) is excluded from distillation projection per the deep reference's distillation-projection note.

findings.claim: The text's social-psychology findings are primarily from Western, educated, industrialised, rich, democratic (WEIRD) populations
findings.failure_mode: source-supported but absent from the deep ref; and the source makes the point about the field (WEIRD societies overstudied), not about the textbook's own findings
findings.evidence: Deep ref has no WEIRD passage. Source 1358-1363 (Ch 1.2, 'Multicultural and Cross-Cultural Psychology'): 'Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan discuss how WEIRD societies have been overstudied and the results have been wrongly applied to non-WEIRD societies (2010)'.
findings.fix: correct: The text itself flags that WEIRD societies have been overstudied and their results wrongly generalised (Ch 1.2, citing Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan 2010) | cycle-to-deep: source 1358-1363

notes: Quotations: all [V] inline quotes (Table 7.3 definitions; FAE 'overemphasize internal factors'/'underestimate the power of the situation') match the converted source (the confirmation-bias row reads 'confrms' in the source, a ligature loss in conversion). Two unmarked quotation-mark passages (D004, D006) are deep-ref paraphrases, not source text. The distillation carries no blockquotes; the protocol asks for 2-5 verbatim blockquotes for open-nc sources and a blockquote in the worked example where source wording carries the claim.
